meta.titre: Interest Rate Determination: liquidity preference and the money market
meta.sous_theme: Demand for money, supply of money and the equilibrium rate of interest

sections.contenu_markdown: A trader in Douala who leaves cash in a drawer earns nothing on it, while a neighbour who lends it through a bank account or buys a bond earns interest. Every day, households and firms decide how much money to keep ready to spend and how much to lend out. Those decisions, together with the actions of the monetary authorities, push the price of borrowing up or down, and a farmer asking for a loan to buy a pump or a firm planning a new workshop feels the result at once. At A Level the topic returns as a table of money balances in which you must find the equilibrium rate, and as an essay on how far interest rates can be controlled.

items: Interest is the payment made for the use of borrowed money, usually stated as a percentage per year.
A bond is a certificate of debt that pays its holder a fixed income for lending money to a borrower.
Liquidity is how easily and quickly an asset can be turned into cash without losing value.

sections.titre: Liquidity preference: how the money market sets the interest rate
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Interest as the price of liquidity
In the Keynesian theory of **liquidity preference**, the rate of interest is the reward for giving up liquidity. It is determined in the money market by the demand for money and the supply of money.

### Demand for money
Keynes identified three motives for holding money.

| Motive | Why money is held | Link with the interest rate |
|---|---|---|
| Transactions | To pay for everyday purchases | Depends mainly on income, not on the rate |
| Precautionary | To meet unexpected expenses | Depends mainly on income, not on the rate |
| Speculative | To avoid a loss on bonds, and to buy them when their price is low | Inverse: balances fall as the rate rises |

Transactions and precautionary money are called **active balances**. Speculative money is called **idle balances**. The speculative demand is inverse because the price of a bond with a fixed income moves in the opposite direction to the interest rate. At a high rate, bond prices are low and expected to rise, so people hold bonds instead of cash. At a low rate, bond prices are high and expected to fall, so people prefer to hold cash, which also costs less in lost interest. At a very low rate the demand for idle money may become perfectly elastic: this is the **liquidity trap**.

### Supply of money
The supply of money is fixed by the central bank and the banking system. In the basic model it is **autonomous**: it does not depend on the rate, so the supply curve is vertical.

### Equilibrium
The equilibrium rate is where total demand for money (active plus idle) equals the supply of money. If the rate is above it, people hold more money than they wish, buy bonds, bond prices rise and the rate falls. If it is below, people want more money than exists, sell bonds, bond prices fall and the rate rises.

A rise in the money supply shifts the supply curve to the right and lowers the rate. A rise in income increases active balances, shifts total demand to the right and raises the rate.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a schedule of speculative balances and a money supply figure are given
variantes.contenu_markdown: Step 1: subtract the active balances from the money supply to find the money available for idle holding. Step 2: find the rate at which the idle demand equals that amount. Step 3: check that active plus idle demand equals the supply. If the amount is not in the table, say that the equilibrium lies between two rates. Keep one unit (thousand or million FCFA) throughout.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks for another theory or for evaluation
variantes.contenu_markdown: The loanable funds approach treats the rate as the price that balances the demand for loanable funds (borrowing by firms for investment, by households and by the government) and the supply of loanable funds (saving, and credit created by banks). A rise in saving lowers the rate; a rise in government borrowing raises it. Liquidity preference stresses the stock of money balances, while loanable funds stresses the flows of saving and borrowing, so the two theories complement each other. In practice rates also differ with risk and the length of the loan, and they include compensation for expected inflation.

variantes.nom: Evaluation: can the central bank control the rate?
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the command is discuss or to what extent
variantes.contenu_markdown: For: the central bank controls the money supply and the rate at which it lends to banks, which influences commercial rates. Against: in a liquidity trap more money does not lower the rate; banks may not pass changes on to customers; expectations of inflation and risk also affect rates; and in Cameroon monetary policy is set for the whole CEMAC area by the BEAC, so national conditions are not the only influence. Conclude with a judgement: control is real but partial, strongest in the short run and over the rates the central bank sets directly.

sections.enonce_markdown:
In a hypothetical economy the transactions and precautionary balances together are 300 million FCFA. The speculative balances demanded at different rates are:

| Rate of interest (%) | Speculative balances (million FCFA) |
|---|---|
| 12 | 100 |
| 10 | 200 |
| 8 | 350 |
| 6 | 550 |
| 4 | 800 |

The money supply is 650 million FCFA.

(a) Calculate the idle balances that the money supply can satisfy.
(b) State the equilibrium rate of interest.
(c) Explain what happens if the rate stands at 10 per cent.
(d) The central bank raises the money supply to 850 million FCFA. Find the new equilibrium rate.

etapes.action: Subtract the active balances from the money supply.
etapes.justification: Active balances are held whatever the rate, so only the rest of the money supply is available as idle balances.
Equilibrium needs idle demand to equal the idle money available.
etapes.resultat_markdown: 350 appears at a rate of 8 per cent, so the equilibrium rate is **8 per cent**.

etapes.justification: At equilibrium total demand for money equals the supply.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $300 + 350 = 650$ million FCFA, which equals the money supply.

etapes.action: Test the rate of 10 per cent.
etapes.justification: Comparing total demand with supply shows the direction of adjustment.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Total demand is $300 + 200 = 500$ million FCFA, so people hold $650 - 500 = 150$ million FCFA more money than they wish. They buy bonds, bond prices rise and the rate falls towards 8 per cent.

etapes.action: Repeat the method for the new money supply.
etapes.justification: The supply curve has shifted to the right, so the idle money available has changed.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $850 - 300 = 550$ million FCFA, which matches 6 per cent. Check: $300 + 550 = 850$. The new rate is **6 per cent**.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) 350 million FCFA. (b) 8 per cent. (c) At 10 per cent there is an excess supply of money of 150 million FCFA, so people buy bonds, bond prices rise and the rate falls to 8 per cent. (d) The increase in the money supply lowers the equilibrium rate to 6 per cent, a fall of 2 percentage points.

items.erreur_markdown: "As the interest rate rises, people hold more money for transactions."
items.pourquoi_faux: Transactions money is needed to pay for everyday purchases and depends mainly on income, not on the rate. Only the speculative demand is sensitive to the rate.
items.correction_markdown: Transactions and precautionary balances (active balances) depend mainly on income. Speculative (idle) balances fall as the rate rises.

items.erreur_markdown: "The money supply is 550. The table shows idle balances of 300 at 5% and 550 at 3%, so the rate is 3%." (the active balances were 250)
items.pourquoi_faux: The student forgot that part of the money supply is already needed for active balances. Only the remainder can meet the idle demand.
items.correction_markdown: Subtract first: $550 - 250 = 300$ is the idle money available, and the rate is read where idle demand equals 300, which is 5%.

items.erreur_markdown: "When the interest rate rises, bond prices rise."
items.pourquoi_faux: A bond pays a fixed income, so a higher market rate means that a buyer pays less for the same income. Bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions.
items.correction_markdown: A rise in the interest rate lowers bond prices; a fall in the rate raises them.

items.erreur_markdown: "A rise in the money supply shifts the speculative demand curve to the right."
items.pourquoi_faux: The money supply and the speculative demand are different curves. A change in the supply of money shifts the supply curve, not the demand curve.
items.correction_markdown: A rise in the money supply shifts the vertical supply curve to the right and, in the normal case, lowers the equilibrium rate of interest.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Name the motive for holding money in each case: (i) a trader keeps cash to pay for daily transport and wages; (ii) a family keeps cash in case of a sudden illness; (iii) an investor keeps cash because she expects bond prices to fall.
(b) A bond pays 6,000 FCFA every year. Calculate its price when the market rate is 8 per cent and when it is 12 per cent, using price = annual income divided by the rate. Explain what the two answers show.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) (i) **Transactions motive**. (ii) **Precautionary motive**. (iii) **Speculative motive**. The first two form active balances and the third forms idle balances.
(b) At 8 per cent: $6\,000 \div 0.08 = 75\,000$ FCFA. At 12 per cent: $6\,000 \div 0.12 = 50\,000$ FCFA. The price is **75,000 FCFA at 8 per cent and 50,000 FCFA at 12 per cent**: when the rate rises the bond price falls, so bond prices and interest rates are inversely related.

items.enonce_markdown:
The table shows the speculative balances demanded in a hypothetical economy (million FCFA).

| Rate of interest (%) | Speculative balances |
|---|---|
| 9 | 150 |
| 7 | 250 |
| 5 | 400 |
| 3 | 600 |

Active balances are 200 million FCFA and the money supply is 600 million FCFA.
(a) Find the equilibrium rate.
(b) The money supply rises by 200 million FCFA. Find the new equilibrium rate.
(c) At 7 per cent, with the original money supply, calculate the excess supply of money and say what happens to the rate.
(d) With the original money supply, active balances rise to 350 million FCFA because incomes grow. Find the new rate.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Idle money available: $600 - 200 = 400$, which matches 5 per cent. The equilibrium rate is **5 per cent**.
(b) New supply 800. Idle money available: $800 - 200 = 600$, which matches 3 per cent. The new rate is **3 per cent**.
(c) At 7 per cent total demand is $200 + 250 = 450$. Supply is 600, so there is an excess supply of money of $600 - 450 = 150$ million FCFA: **150 million FCFA**. People buy bonds, bond prices rise and the rate falls.
(d) Idle money available: $600 - 350 = 250$, which matches 7 per cent. The rate rises from 5 to **7 per cent**, because higher income increases active balances and leaves less money for idle holding.

items.enonce_markdown:
In a hypothetical economy active balances are 300 million FCFA. The demand for idle balances is 400 million FCFA at a rate of 6 per cent, 600 at 4 per cent and 800 at 2 per cent. At a rate of 1 per cent, people are willing to hold any amount of idle money.
(a) Find the equilibrium rate when the money supply is 700, 900, 1,100, 1,300 and 1,600 million FCFA.
(b) Explain why the rate stops falling.
(c) Discuss to what extent a central bank can lower interest rates by increasing the money supply. (8 marks)
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Idle money available is 400, 600, 800, 1,000 and 1,300 million FCFA. The rates are **6 per cent, 4 per cent, 2 per cent, 1 per cent and 1 per cent**. At a money supply of 1,300 the idle money available (1,000) exceeds the 800 demanded at 2 per cent, so the rate falls to 1 per cent, where demand is perfectly elastic.
(b) At 1 per cent bond prices are so high that people expect them to fall and prefer cash, so extra money is simply held as idle balances and the demand curve is horizontal: this is the liquidity trap.
(c) Award marks for: the central bank controls the money supply, and a larger supply normally lowers the rate (2); lower rates may raise investment and consumption (1); the liquidity trap limits the effect at very low rates (2); banks may not lend or pass the cut on, and expectations of risk or inflation also matter (2); a reasoned conclusion that control is real but partial (1).

items_markdown: In liquidity preference theory the interest rate is set where the demand for money equals the supply of money.

Transactions and precautionary money (active balances) depend on income; speculative money (idle balances) is inversely related to the rate because bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions.
To read a table, subtract the active balances from the money supply, then find the rate where idle demand equals the remainder.
A rise in the money supply lowers the rate; a rise in income raises active balances and the rate. At a very low rate the liquidity trap stops the rate falling.
The loanable funds approach gives a complementary view, and central bank control of the rate is real but limited.
